query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In bare Q235 steel, the initial surface microstructure heterogeneity—especially the density and distribution of inclusions and irregular grain boundaries—governs the early formation and stability of a passive iron oxide film. A more uniform microstructure promotes rapid, continuous passivation that suppresses localized pitting in harsh chloride‐containing environments, while a heterogeneous microstructure induces localized breakdown of the passive film and accelerates corrosion degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with its native microstructural features (grain boundaries, inclusions, and associated defects) prior to any exposure.
generation.intervention: A controlled surface treatment (e.g., careful polishing and/or thermal pre-treatment or annealing) designed to reduce microstructural heterogeneity by homogenizing the distribution of inclusions and grain boundary character.
generation.conditions: Exposure to a simulated harsh environment such as a 3.5 wt.% NaCl aqueous solution at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (e.g., ~70°C) to mimic aggressive corrosion conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniformity and continuity of the resultant passive iron oxide (likely Fe3O4/Fe2O3) layer, which forms preferentially on more homogeneous areas versus being disrupted at localized anodic sites associated with microstructural heterogeneity.
generation.mechanism: Heterogeneous microstructural zones (e.g., regions with clustered non-metallic inclusions or irregular grain boundaries) act as localized anodic sites that hinder the formation of a coherent passive film. In contrast, a more uniform surface accelerates and stabilizes passivation. This difference drives a variation in local electrochemical behavior, altering the overall corrosion kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples that receive the surface treatment will form a more continuous and protective oxide film, resulting in lower corrosion current densities, reduced mass loss, and attenuated pitting (as seen in polarization and EIS measurements) compared to untreated Q235 steel in both room temperature and moderately elevated temperature tests.
generation.baseline: Untreated, as-received Q235 steel showing its native heterogeneous microstructure and passive film formation behavior.
generation.boundary: Observations are expected in chloride-containing aggressive environments at moderate temperatures (<100°C), where the kinetics of oxide formation and breakdown are most sensitive to local microstructural features; effects outside these conditions may not follow the same trends.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative effect of microstructural homogenization on corrosion rates may depend on other factors (e.g., residual stresses or specific inclusion chemistry), and additional complexities such as the role of atmospheric oxygen during exposure remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples. One set undergoes a controlled surface treatment (polishing followed by annealing to promote homogenization), while the control group remains as-received. Subject both sets to immersion tests in a standardized 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (e.g., 70°C) for identical durations. Monitor corrosion kinetics using electrochemical techniques such as potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and quantify mass loss after exposure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the surface-treated (homogenized) Q235 steel does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance (i.e., lower icorr, higher Rct, reduced mass loss and pitting features) compared to the untreated specimens under the identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis that microstructural uniformity promotes more protective passivation and thereby suppresses corrosion-related degradation will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this paper, the CoCrFeNiTix HEA coatings are prepared on Q235 steel substrate by laser cladding. The effect of Ti content on the microstructure and corrosion resistance in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution was studied. Furthermore, the corrosion resistance mechanism was analyzed experimentally and by first-principles calculations.
